newsitem.title: COMOROS: Secessionists on Moheli island elect "president".
newsitem.headline: Secessionists on Moheli island elect "president".

text.p: Secessionists on the Moheli island elected a former army officer as "president" of their self-declared breakaway state on Monday, the second island in the Comoros archipelago to declare independence in 10 days.
The secessionists at a rally in the Moheli capital Fromboni chose Said Mohamed Souef as their president and he then named fellow former army officer Sodri Ahmed as prime minister, witnesses said.
"Our island has been permanently exploited and deprived of its wealth in favour of Grand Comoro," Souef told a crowd in front of Fromboni prefecture. "We are today taking our destiny in our hands."
Moheli is the smallest of the three islands in the Comoro archipelago and has some 25,000 people. The Comoro Islands, now with a population of 670,000, became independent from France in 1975.
All shops, markets and government offices were closed on Moheli on Monday for a general strike called by the new leaders while French flags raised by supporters flew from buildings.
Secessionists later seized control of the office of the island's governor and cut the telephone lines, witnesses said.
Moheli secessionists have the same complaints as comrades on the island of Anjouan, the second largest island in the Comoros and the first to declare at the start of August it was breaking away.
An Organisation of African Unity (OAU) mediator arrived on Monday in Anjouan for talks amid hopes among some diplomats he could defuse the row between the islands and Comoran capital of Moroni.

The OAU said last week envoy Pierre Yere of Ivory Coast would discuss measures to defuse tension "while addressing the legitimate concerns of the islanders while maintaining the unity, territorial integrity and cohesion" of Comoros.

Chanting anti-Comoran government slogans, thousands of people gathered at Anjouan airport to greet Yere, who was welcomed by 75-year-old Foundi Abdallah Ibrahim, a former Islamic preacher who was elected "president" last Tuesday.
"I am optimistic," Yere said on Sunday after his first talks with the Comoron government and secessionists by telephone.
Yere also said on Sunday Comoran government leaders had told him they had sent no troops to Anjouan to suppress the revolt.

The two islands had demanded a return to French rule, saying they had nothing but poverty, largely centralised government and coups since independence. France has refused to back their drive for separation from the Federal Islamic Republic of the Comoros.

"Federalism is just a name but in practice it is a highly centralised system," a Moheli secessionist told Reuters by telephone on Monday, complaining government and army posts were unfairly shared out and his island received little funding.
The poverty in Anjouan and Moheli contrasts with the comparative prosperity on the nearby island of Mayotte, which voted against independence in 1975 and remains French.
To the annoyance of Comoran islanders, local broadcasts of programmes from French radio and television stations were cut and official Comoran radio has made no mention of the crisis.
Three people including a gendarme were killed on July 14 -- Bastille Day -- as demonstrators, pressing for Anjouan to return to French rule or be independent, clashed with security forces.
